title: Venn Diagrams
summary: Two question families: (1) region arithmetic — count union, intersection, only-regions, exactly-two, neither using inclusion-exclusion over labelled Venn regions; (2) relation selection — decide whether categories nest (definitional necessity), stay apart (impossibility) or intersect (possible but not forced). The arithmetic family is pure formula discipline; the relation family is two quick tests per pair. Label every region before computing and both become near-90% accuracy topics.

subtopics.title: What a Venn diagram encodes
subtopics.concept:
A Venn diagram is a picture of set membership: every point inside a circle belongs to that category; overlap regions belong to both. Two habits solve most CGL venn questions:

1. **Region bookkeeping.** Name the 4 regions of a two-circle diagram (only A, only B, both, neither) and the 8 regions of a three-circle one. Every question is a sum or difference of named regions.
2. **Relation reading.** 'Choose the right diagram for X, Y, Z' asks about *definitional* relations: is one category ALWAYS inside another (nested circles)? Can they NEVER meet (separate circles)? Otherwise (overlap possible but not forced) draw intersecting circles.

Draw the regions and label them with the given numbers before computing — unlabelled diagrams cause double-counting errors.

formulas.name: Two-set inclusion-exclusion
formulas.note: The intersection is counted twice on the right, so subtract once.

formulas.name: Only-regions
formulas.note: 'Only A' is A minus the overlap.

tricks.title: Label regions, don’t imagine them
tricks.body: Write the numbers INTO the regions: |A∩B| in the lens, only-A and only-B in the moons, neither outside. Sums become single looks instead of formula recalls.

example.q:
**Q.** 60 students; 35 like tea, 30 coffee, 10 both. How many like neither?

**Sol.** Tea-only 25 + both 10 + coffee-only 20 = 55 inside; 60 − 55 = **5**.
example.solution: Fill the diagram first; the answer is whatever region is left empty times its count.

mistakes: Counting the intersection twice when totalling.
Treating 'like tea' (including both) as 'like only tea'.
Forgetting the 'neither' region sits outside both circles.

subtopics.title: Two-circle counting
subtopics.concept:
With two sets there are exactly four regions: only A, only B, both, neither. Every two-circle question is a sum or difference of these:

- **Union** (at least one) = only A + only B + both.
- **Only A** = |A| − both; **Only B** = |B| − both.
- **Neither** = grand total − union.

Exam data typically gives |A|, |B| and the overlap (or hides one of them behind the union). Rearranging the inclusion-exclusion identity recovers any missing region in one step.

formulas.name: Two-set inclusion-exclusion
formulas.note: The intersection is counted twice on the right, so subtract once.

formulas.name: Only-regions
formulas.note: 'Only A' is A minus the overlap.

tricks.title: Label regions, don’t imagine them
tricks.body: Write the numbers INTO the regions: the lens, the two moons, and outside. Sums become single looks instead of formula recalls.

example.q:
**Q.** 60 students; 35 like tea, 30 coffee, 10 both. How many like neither?

**Sol.** Tea-only 25 + both 10 + coffee-only 20 = 55 inside; 60 − 55 = **5**.
example.solution: Fill the diagram first; the answer is whatever region is left, counted.

mistakes: Counting the intersection twice when totalling.
Treating 'like tea' (including both) as 'like only tea'.
Forgetting the 'neither' region sits outside both circles.

subtopics.title: Three-circle counting
subtopics.concept:
With three sets A, B, C the master formula is

|A∪B∪C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A∩B| − |B∩C| − |A∩C| + |A∩B∩C|.

Two derived region-counts appear constantly:

- **Exactly two** = (|A∩B| − all3) + (|B∩C| − all3) + (|A∩C| − all3): each pairwise figure includes the triple region, which must be stripped from both pairs it contaminates.
- **Exactly one** = union − exactly-two − all-three.

Exam data usually gives the seven numbers directly (three singles, three pairs, one triple); plug them into the 8 regions and add or subtract as asked.

formulas.name: Three-set union
formulas.note: Add singles, subtract pairs, re-add the triple.

formulas.name: Exactly two sets
formulas.note: Sum of the three pairwise figures minus three times the triple.

formulas.name: Exactly one set
formulas.note: Strip the multi-set members from the union.

tricks.title: Triple-strip subtraction
tricks.body: Whenever a question says 'exactly two', your reflex is: pairwise sums overcount the core by 3. Compute pairwise sums, subtract 3×(all three), done.

example.solution: 'Exactly' always means: subtract every richer region, as many times as it was counted.

mistakes: Using pairwise figures as 'exactly two' without stripping the triple region.
Sign slips on the +all-three term in the union formula.
Adding 'neither/none' into the union before subtracting from the grand total.

subtopics.title: Choosing the correct diagram
subtopics.concept:
For 'Which diagram represents Doctors, Men, Writers?' style questions, decide each pair with two tests:

1. **Necessity test** — is every X definitionally a Y? (Every mother is a female.) → circle of X drawn **inside** Y.
2. **Impossibility test** — can X and Y never share a member? (A square and a triangle.) → **separate** circles.
3. Otherwise — overlap possible but neither forced (doctors and writers) → **intersecting** circles.

Same-type categories usually intersect; category-of-category pairs (squares/rectangles/polygons) nest; mutually exclusive definitions separate.

tricks.title: Test one pair at a time
tricks.body: Never judge the whole picture at once. Run necessity/impossibility on each pair; the correct option is the only one agreeing on every pair.

example.q:
**Q.** Mothers, Females, Engineers.

**Sol.** Mothers ⊂ Females (necessity). Engineers ∩ Females possible (female engineers) and Engineers ⊄ Females (male engineers) → intersecting. Match the option reflecting both facts.
example.solution: One wrong pair eliminates an option — work pair by pair until one option survives.

mistakes: Drawing engineers inside females because most examples in mind are female.
Missing a third category's relation to the nested pair.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two circles, find neither / only-one / union.
Seven region numbers, find union or none.
Union and two regions given; find the intersection.
pyqPatterns.approach: Rearrange |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − x for the unknown region.
Same formulas on percentages; neither = 100 − union%.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three categories; pick the correct circle arrangement.
pyqPatterns.approach: Per-pair necessity/impossibility tests; eliminate options pair-wise.

solvedExamples.q: In a class of **60 students, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 10 like both.** How many students like **neither** tea nor coffee?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add both counts, subtract the overlap once, subtract from the total.

solvedExamples.q: In a survey, **8 people read A and B, 7 read B and C, 6 read A and C, and 3 read all three.** How many read **exactly two** papers?
solvedExamples.solution: (8 − 3) + (7 − 3) + (6 − 3) = **12**. Each pairwise figure wrongly includes the triple readers.

solvedExamples.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Doctors, Men and Writers**?
options: Doctors and Writers both inside the Men circle
Doctors inside Men; Writers a separate circle
solvedExamples.solution: No category is definitionally inside another (a doctor need not be a man; men need not write), and none is impossible to combine. So all three circles pairwise intersect.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Run necessity (nesting) and impossibility (separation) tests pair by pair; neither applies here.

solvedExamples.q: Of **200 people, 90 drink coffee, 80 tea, 70 milk; 40 coffee and tea, 35 tea and milk, 30 coffee and milk; 15 all three.** How many drink **none**?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add singles, subtract pairs, re-add triple, subtract from total.

practice.q: In a group, **|A ∪ B| = 40**, the number of elements in **A only is 15** and in **B only is 12**. How many elements are in **both A and B**?
practice.solution: Union = only-A + only-B + both → 40 = 15 + 12 + both → both = **13**.
practice.shortcut: The three inside-regions sum to the union.

practice.q: In a school, **40 students play hockey, 25 play cricket and 12 play both.** How many students play **hockey or cricket** (at least one)?
In a survey, **70% of people watch cricket, 60% watch football and 40% watch both.** What percentage watch **neither**?
practice.shortcut: Percentages behave exactly like counts — total is 100.

practice.q: In a class of **80 students, every student plays at least one of chess and carrom. 50 play chess and 40 play carrom.** How many play **both**?
practice.shortcut: 'Everyone plays' pins the union equal to the class strength.
Sum, subtract pairs, re-add the triple.

practice.q: In a colony of newspaper readers, **45 people read the Herald, 25 read both the Herald and the Tribune.** How many read **only the Herald**?

A club's three sports sections show: **15 members in badminton only, 10 in tennis only, 8 in chess only, 6 in badminton and tennis only, 5 in tennis and chess only, 4 in badminton and chess only, and 2 in all three.** How many members play **at least one** of the three sports?
practice.solution: The seven regions are disjoint — add them: 15+10+8+6+5+4+2 = **50**.
practice.shortcut: When every region is given 'only'-style, no formula — just add.

practice.q: Given **|A| = 22, |B| = 19, |C| = 17, |A∩B| = 9, |B∩C| = 7, |A∩C| = 6, |A∩B∩C| = 4** — how many elements belong to **exactly one** set?
practice.solution: Exactly two = (9−4)+(7−4)+(6−4) = 10. Exactly one = union − exactly two − triple = 40 − 10 − 4 = **26**.
practice.shortcut: Union minus everyone in two or three sets.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Squares, Rectangles and Polygons**?
options: Squares inside Rectangles, both inside Polygons
Squares and Rectangles intersecting, both inside Polygons
practice.solution: Every square is a rectangle and every rectangle is a polygon — a fully nested chain of circles.
practice.shortcut: Necessity test passes for every pair → nested circles.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Mothers, Females and Engineers**?
options: Mothers inside Females; Engineers circle intersecting both
practice.solution: Every mother is definitionally a female → Mothers inside Females. Engineers can be male or female and may or may not be mothers → the Engineers circle crosses both.
practice.shortcut: Definition decides nesting; possibility decides intersection.

practice.q: **|A ∩ B| = 8, |A − B| = 10, |B| = 20 and 7 elements belong to neither set.** What is the size of the **universal set** (all elements considered)?
practice.shortcut: Four disjoint regions: both, A-only, B-only, neither.

practice.q: **|A| = 25, |B| = 20 and |A ∩ B| = 8.** How many elements are in **exactly one** of A and B?
practice.shortcut: Strip the lens from each circle and add the moons.

practice.q: In a batch of **120 trainees: 55 know Python, 45 know Java, 40 know C++; 20 know Python and Java, 18 know Java and C++, 15 know Python and C++; 8 know all three.** How many trainees know **none** of the three?
practice.shortcut: Full inclusion-exclusion, then subtract from the batch.

practice.q: **|A∩B| = 12, |B∩C| = 10, |A∩C| = 9 and |A∩B∩C| = 5.** How many elements belong to **at least two** of the sets?
practice.solution: At least two = exactly two + all three = (12−5)+(10−5)+(9−5) + 5 = 7+5+4+5 = **21**. Shortcut: pairwise sum 31 counts the triple 3 times → 31 − 2×5 = 21.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Words, English words and Hindi words**?
options: English words inside Words; Hindi words a separate circle outside
All three nested inside one another
English and Hindi circles inside Words, not overlapping each other
practice.solution: Both are subsets of Words (necessity), and a word cannot be English and Hindi at once (impossibility) → two disjoint circles inside the big one.
practice.shortcut: One pair needs the impossibility test — the other two are simple nestings.
